correctness.rationale: At minimizing parallel supporting lines in the plane, either two integer vertices (distance ≥1) or a supporting primitive edge and an integer opposite support vertex give a nonzero integer determinant over the primitive edge norm, hence distance ≥1/sqrt(M(a,b)). For every maximizing positive primitive (p,q), modular inverse produces lattice (x,y) with p y−q x=1 inside [0,p]×[0,q] and strictly interior orthogonal projection to segment (0,0)−(p,q); distance equals 1/sqrt(M). Equalities force primitive maximal direction, determinant one, and projection contact; conversely those contacts attain the bound. A corner is primitive iff gcd(a,b)=1. For a=28t,b=36t, t≡1 mod21, gcd(a−1,b−1)=1; the top three candidates on each boundary side share nontrivial factors (4t/7/2 or 4t/3/2). Remaining side candidates are strictly inferior by differences 88t−7 and 40t−7. Independent exhaustive primitive searches for t=1,22,43 reproduced unique maxima (27,35),(615,791),(1203,1547), and determinant witness (10,13) at t=1.
residual_risks: An exact finite enumeration for three t values and small rectangles cannot establish the infinite t-class; those rely on gcd/divisibility and norm-gap inequalities.
The equality formulation presumes disjoint polytopes, not arbitrary convex bodies or non-Euclidean norms.

value.rationale: Replacing a square with an anisotropic integer rectangle is a natural variant of the established kissing-polytopes invariant. A complete optimal formula and equality conditions for all a,b reduce geometry to arithmetic, while an explicit infinite interior-extremizer family disproves naive side-boundary search. The distinction is substantive: Euclidean distance is not preserved by rectangular normalization.
residual_risks: The maximization is finite arithmetic rather than a simple closed expression for arbitrary a,b; no arbitrary lattice, norm or dimension claim.
